bai.ten: Orbits: moving straight through curved spacetime
bai.moTa: Newton’s ellipse slowly turns: Mercury, the star S2, and orbits close to a black hole
bai.yChinh: A planet is not “pulled” toward the Sun; it follows a **geodesic**, the straightest possible path through curved spacetime. The orbit we see is the shadow of a world line shaped like a coil spring. Newton says an orbit is a closed ellipse; Einstein adds a small extra term that makes the ellipse slowly turn, and close to a black hole no stable circular orbit exists inside 3 rs.
bai.giaiThich:
- An orbit is the shadow in space of a four-dimensional geodesic (Lesson 10).
    - The Schwarzschild metric does not change with time or with rotation about the center, so two quantities are conserved: the energy $E$ and the angular momentum $L$.
    - Einstein’s effective potential has an extra term $-GML^2/(c^2r^3)$. It turns the ellipse by an angle $\Delta\varphi = 6\pi GM/[c^2a(1-e^2)]$ on every orbit.
    - Mercury: 42.98″ per century (Einstein, November 1915). The star S2: about 12′ per orbit (GRAVITY 2020).
    - Around a non-rotating black hole the innermost stable circular orbit lies at 3 rs; gas that spirals in to that point releases 5.7% of its rest mass.
bai.conSo.1: **42.98″ per century**: the general-relativistic precession of Mercury (0.1035″ per orbit). The ellipse needs about 3 million years to turn through a full circle.
bai.conSo.2: **12′ per orbit**: the precession of the star S2 around Sagittarius A*, about 7,000 times Mercury’s.
bai.conSo.3: **3 rs**: the innermost stable circular orbit around a non-rotating black hole; an object there moves at half the speed of light.
bai.conSo.4: **5.7%**: the fraction of rest mass radiated away as gas spirals in from far away down to 3 rs, 8 times the yield of hydrogen fusion (0.7%).
bai.hieuDung: **What does “moving straight” mean?** A flight from Tokyo to Los Angeles curves north toward Alaska: that is the shortest route on a sphere, so it is “straight” in the sense of a curved surface. A planet is the same: it does not turn, nothing pushes it, it simply goes straight through four-dimensional spacetime. And do not picture it as a marble rolling on Flamm’s paraboloid: a marble rolls only because Earth’s gravity pulls it down. The elliptical shape of the orbit comes mainly from **curved time**; the precession comes from curved time and curved space together.
bai.nguon: Mercury’s orbit: NASA/JPL orbital elements (Standish and Williams). Star S2: GRAVITY Collaboration 2018, A&A 615, L15 and 2020, A&A 636, L5. Constants: CODATA 2018, IAU 2012. The paths in the model are numerical solutions of the Schwarzschild geodesic equation.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Explain why an orbit is the shadow of a geodesic in four-dimensional spacetime.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Say where the two conserved quantities $E$ and $L$ come from, and read an effective-potential graph.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Calculate Mercury’s perihelion precession with the formula $6\pi GM/[c^2a(1-e^2)]$.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Explain why a black hole has an innermost stable circular orbit at 3 rs, and why a gas disk has an inner edge.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Distinguish the time of a distant clock from an object’s own proper time as it falls into a black hole.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.ten: An orbit is the shadow of a world line
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
You are watching an object fly around a black hole, drawn the way we did in Lesson 4. The horizontal grid is space **right now** (with one dimension left out). The vertical direction is **time**, measured by a clock very far away; the lower you go, the further into the past.

The bright blue line plunging downward is the object’s {{đường thế giới|world line}}: a coil spring. The orange-red tube in the middle is the {{chân trời sự kiện|event horizon}} as time passes. The faint trail on the grid is the spring’s shadow, the thing we usually call the orbit.

Lesson 10 showed that an object in {{rơi tự do|free fall}} follows a {{đường trắc địa|geodesic}}, the “straightest” path through spacetime, the one along which proper time is longest. A planet is simply in free fall too. No string pulls it; it goes straight through curved spacetime, and the shadow of that straight path in space is a nearly closed loop.

> [Lưu ý] The picture leaves out one dimension of space and **squeezes the time axis** so that each turn of the spring fits in the frame. At true scale the spring is stretched out almost straight, as in Lesson 4.

> [Thử ngay] [[See the world line|ktg]] [[See the shadow on Flamm’s paraboloid|mat]] [[View from above|tren]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: The Schwarzschild metric and two conserved quantities
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Now the orbit lies on **Flamm’s paraboloid** from Lesson 11. To calculate the path we need a “distance map” of spacetime around the mass: the {{metric Schwarzschild|Schwarzschild metric}}. In the plane of the orbit:

$$ \dd s^2 = -\Big(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\Big)c^2\dd t^2 + \frac{\dd r^2}{1-r_s/r} + r^2\dd\varphi^2 $$

$t$ is the time of a clock very far away, $r$ is the radius (the circumference of a circle divided by $2\pi$), $\varphi$ is the angle around the center, and $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ is the Schwarzschild radius. The first term is curved time (Lesson 9); the second is curved space (Lesson 11).

The coefficients do not change with $t$ and do not change with $\varphi$. These two symmetries give two quantities that **stay fixed along the whole orbit**:

$$ E = \Big(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\Big)\frac{\dd t}{\dd\tau}, \qquad L = r^2\,\frac{\dd\varphi}{\dd\tau} $$

$\tau$ is the object’s {{thời gian riêng|proper time}}. $E$ is the {{năng lượng riêng|specific energy}} (in units of $mc^2$) and $L$ is the {{mô-men động lượng riêng|specific angular momentum}}. For the orbit now running, $E = 0{,}973$ and $L = 2{,}13\,r_s c$. An $E$ below 1 means the object is **bound**: it cannot escape to great distances.

> [Thử ngay] The data box at the lower left compares the object’s clock with the distant clock: the object’s clock is always slower. [[View from above|tren]] [[Oblique view|cheo]]

> [Lưu ý] **Sound**: a sustained note follows the object’s speed. Its frequency is 200 Hz times the speed ratio (relative to the speed at the farthest point) raised to the power 0.6, so the note swoops up each time the object rushes through the closest point and drops as it moves away. Each pass through the closest point also rings a bell. This is a conversion for the ear; the power 0.6 compresses the range of speeds so it is pleasant to hear.

+++ Going deeper: why a symmetry gives a conserved quantity
A geodesic is the path along which proper time $\tau = \int \sqrt{-\dd s^2}/c$ is longest. Write $\dot{x} = \dd x/\dd\tau$ and use units with $c = 1$. The function to make stationary is

$$ \mathcal{L} = -\Big(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\Big)\dot t^2 + \frac{\dot r^2}{1-r_s/r} + r^2\dot\varphi^2 $$

The Euler–Lagrange equation for $t$ reads $\frac{\dd}{\dd\tau}\big(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\dot t\big) = \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial t = 0$, because $\mathcal{L}$ does not contain $t$. So $(1-r_s/r)\,\dot t$ is constant: that is $E$. The same argument for $\varphi$ gives $r^2\dot\varphi = L$.

There is one more relation: the four-velocity has a fixed “length”, $\mathcal{L} = -1$. Substituting $\dot t = E/(1-r_s/r)$ and $\dot\varphi = L/r^2$:

$$ \dot r^2 = E^2 - \Big(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\Big)\Big(1+\frac{L^2}{r^2}\Big) $$

Check with numbers at the closest point, $r = 4{,}83\,r_s$: $(1 - 1/4{,}83)(1 + 4{,}54/23{,}3) = 0{,}947 = 0{,}973^2$. Correct: there the object stops moving inward, $\dot r = 0$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.ten: The effective potential: Einstein adds one term
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
Look at the small graph under **Model controls** below. The last relation of the previous step can be rewritten as the motion of a marble on a slope:

$$ \frac12\Big(\frac{\dd r}{\dd\tau}\Big)^2 + V(r) = \frac{E^2-1}{2} $$

$$ V(r) = -\frac{GM}{r} + \frac{L^2}{2r^2} - \frac{GML^2}{c^2r^3} $$

$V(r)$ is the {{thế hiệu dụng|effective potential}}. The first two terms are exactly Newton’s: the attraction $-GM/r$ pulls in and the “centrifugal” term $L^2/2r^2$ pushes out. The third term is **Einstein’s new part**. It always pulls inward, and it grows very fast as $r$ gets small.

On the graph: the gray curve is Newton, the blue curve is Einstein, and the yellow line is the energy level. The object can only be where the blue curve lies below the yellow line, and it moves back and forth between those two edges.

> [Con số] The new term divided by the centrifugal term is exactly $r_s/r$. At 7 rs it is 1/7. At Mercury it is only about **one part in twenty million**.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the tip of the yellow arrow (the launch velocity) and let go to launch the object yourself; drag the yellow dot at the base of the arrow to change the launch point. While you drag, a dashed line shows the path the object will take; when you let go, the energy line on the graph changes to match.
> [[Rosette orbit|hoa]] [[Orbit close to the black hole|manh]]

+++ Going deeper: from the previous step’s relation to $V(r)$, and why the ellipse does not close
Expand: $(1-r_s/r)(1+L^2/r^2) = 1 - r_s/r + L^2/r^2 - r_sL^2/r^3$. Subtract 1, divide by 2, and substitute $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ (here $c = 1$) to get $V(r)$ above.

In Newton’s theory, the time the object takes to go from the closest point out to the farthest point and back is **exactly equal** to the time it takes to go once around. This is special to a $1/r^2$ force, and it is why the ellipse closes.

For a nearly circular orbit of radius $r$, Einstein gives an in-and-out frequency $\kappa$ and an orbital frequency $\Omega$ related by

$$ \kappa^2 = \Omega^2\Big(1 - \frac{3r_s}{r}\Big) $$

The in-and-out oscillation is slower than the revolution, so between two passes through the closest point the object sweeps an angle $2\pi/\sqrt{1-3r_s/r}$, more than one full turn. The excess is approximately $3\pi r_s/r = 6\pi GM/(c^2r)$. At $r = 3\,r_s$, $\kappa = 0$: the in-and-out oscillation disappears and circular orbits stop being stable (step 7).
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: Launch the object yourself so that it moves in a **nearly circular** orbit: eccentricity below 0.08 (see the “Launch it yourself” card in the control panel).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.goiY: The arrow must be horizontal (perpendicular to the radius) and exactly as long as the circular-orbit speed at the launch point; hover over the dot at the base of the arrow to see the number. At the default launch point (12.7 r<sub>s</sub>) it is about 20.6% of c. When you succeed, the energy line on the graph sits right at the bottom of the well.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
The model now shows **Mercury**. The dashed gray curve is Newton’s ellipse; the blue curve is Einstein’s ellipse, turning very slowly. The point closest to the Sun (the perihelion) gradually shifts: that is {{tiến động cận điểm|perihelion precession}}.

$$ \Delta\varphi = \frac{6\pi GM}{c^2a(1-e^2)} $$

$\Delta\varphi$ is the angle turned on each orbit, $a$ is the semi-major axis, $e$ is the eccentricity (how elongated the ellipse is), and $GM/c^2$ for the Sun is 1.477 km.

> [Ví dụ] Mercury: $a = 57{,}9$ million km, $e = 0{,}2056$. Substituting: $\Delta\varphi = 6\pi \times 1{,}477 / (57{,}9\times10^6 \times 0{,}958) \approx 5{,}0\times10^{-7}$ rad $= 0{,}1035″$ per orbit. A century holds 415.2 orbits, which add up to **42.98″**. The ellipse needs about 3 million years to turn through a full circle.

> [Lịch sử] In 1859 Urbain Le Verrier, the man who had predicted Neptune, found that Mercury’s perihelion turned faster than the other planets could account for under Newton’s laws. The leftover, later pinned down at about 43″ per century, had no explanation; he even guessed at a hidden planet called Vulcan, but no one ever found it. In November 1915 Einstein did the calculation with his new theory and got exactly 43″, without adjusting any parameter.

> [Lưu ý] The model is running extremely fast: hundreds of thousands of orbits per second. The shape of the ellipse is true to scale; the Sun and Mercury are drawn many times larger than they really are so you can see them. The fading trail behind the ellipse marks where the ellipse has just been. The Mercury dot moves fast near the Sun and slowly far away, as in reality, but its pace is slowed right down compared with how fast the ellipse is being fast-forwarded.
> [[Run at 200,000 orbits per second|cham]] [[Run at 5 million orbits per second|nhanh]]

+++ Going deeper: deriving the formula from the orbit equation
Set $u = 1/r$, switch from $\tau$ to $\varphi$ using $\dd\varphi/\dd\tau = Lu^2$, and differentiate the relation from step 2 with respect to $\varphi$. In units with $G = c = 1$, the orbit equation becomes

$$ u'' + u = \frac{M}{L^2} + 3Mu^2 $$

Drop the term $3Mu^2$ and you have Newton’s equation, with solution $u_0 = \frac{M}{L^2}(1 + e\cos\varphi)$: a closed ellipse.

The term $3Mu^2$ is very small. Substituting $u_0$ into it, the only part that matters is $\frac{6M^3e}{L^4}\cos\varphi$, which “resonates” with the left side and gives the approximate solution

$$ u \approx \frac{M}{L^2}\Big[1 + e\cos\Big(\varphi\big(1 - \tfrac{3M^2}{L^2}\big)\Big)\Big] $$

The object returns to the closest point when the angle in parentheses increases by $2\pi$, that is, when $\varphi$ increases by $2\pi/(1-3M^2/L^2) \approx 2\pi + 6\pi M^2/L^2$. For an ellipse $L^2/M = a(1-e^2)$, so the excess is $6\pi M/[a(1-e^2)]$. Restoring $G$ and $c$ gives the formula above.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: The star S2: a test around the black hole at the center of the Milky Way
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Now we have **the star S2**, orbiting Sagittarius A*, the black hole of about 4.3 million solar masses at the center of the Milky Way (Lesson 2). Its orbit is very elongated ($e = 0{,}88$): one orbit takes 16.05 years, and at its closest it is only about **120 AU** from the black hole, roughly 1,400 rs.

At the closest point S2 moves at about **7,700 km/s**, 2.6% of the speed of light. Gravity there is much stronger than at Mercury, so the ellipse turns **about 12′ per orbit**: some 7,000 times Mercury’s rate.

> [Lịch sử] The GRAVITY team combines four large telescopes in Chile into one. In 2018 they measured the light of S2 shifted toward the red exactly as gravitational time dilation (Lesson 9) plus the Doppler effect predict. In 2020 they measured the ellipse turning: the ratio of the measurement to Einstein’s prediction is 1.10 ± 0.19.

> [Thử ngay] The model runs at 20 orbits per second, that is, 320 years per second. Listen to the sustained note: it swoops up each time S2 rushes through the closest point. [[Slow: 2 orbits per second|cham]] [[20 orbits per second|nhanh]]

> [Lưu ý] Here we are looking from very far away: the real black hole would be only a dot; the black hole and S2 are drawn larger than they really are so you can see them. At this distance Flamm’s paraboloid is almost flat.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.ten: Close to a black hole: rosettes and zoom-whirls
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Close to the black hole, the formula from step 4 is no longer enough. The model computes the geodesic directly, and the orbit becomes a **rosette**: each time the object comes back, the closest point (the yellow dot) has turned through a large angle.

- The orbit **close to the black hole** (closest approach 4.83 rs): turns 117.4° per orbit. The formula $6\pi GM/[c^2a(1-e^2)]$ gives only 77.1°.
- The **rosette** orbit (closest approach 2.94 rs): the petals turn very quickly.
- The **zoom-whirl-and-fly-out** orbit (closest approach 2.27 rs): the object winds **more than two and a half times** around the black hole before moving away.

The effective-potential graph explains the third kind. The energy level (the yellow line) sits just below the peak of the blue curve. Near the peak the slope is almost flat, so the object creeps inward very slowly along the radius while still circling fast. It “hovers” there for several turns before sliding back out. This is called a {{quỹ đạo lượn sát|zoom-whirl orbit}}.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the velocity arrow on the left to launch the object yourself: a little less speed makes the rosette turn faster, and a little less again makes the object fall in.
> [[Rosette|hoa]] [[Zoom-whirl, then fly out|xoay]] [[Close to the black hole|manh]] [[See the world line|ktg]]

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “Close to a black hole the pull is so strong that an object has to fall in.” Not true: with enough angular momentum the object can still fly out, even from 2.27 rs. From far away, a black hole pulls no harder than a star of the same mass. Only once the object drops below the peak of the potential is there no way back out.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.de: Launch the object so that its pericenter turns exactly **90° per orbit** (± 8°): the orbit draws a four-petal flower.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.goiY: The closer the object comes to the black hole, the more its pericenter turns. From the default launch point (11.75 r<sub>s</sub>), keep the arrow horizontal and try speeds around 19% of c; while you drag, the label under the arrow shows the turning angle.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
The object is circling at exactly **3 rs**, at **half the speed of light** (as measured by someone standing still at that spot). Its clock runs at 70.7% of the rate of a distant clock.

On the graph, the well and the peak of the blue curve have merged into one: there is no dip left for the object to rest in. This is the {{quỹ đạo tròn ổn định trong cùng|innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO)}}. Inside 3 rs circular orbits still exist, down to 1.5 rs, but they are all **unstable**: the slightest nudge and the object falls.

> [Thử ngay] [[Nudge it inward|cham]] and watch the object spiral in. [[Reset the circular orbit|isco]]
> Or drag the dot at the base of the arrow inside 3 rs and try to launch the object into a circle: however carefully you tune it, it only circles for a little while before falling in or flying off.

So gas orbiting a black hole cannot move in circles below 3 rs. The gas disk has an **inner edge** there (Lesson 15). Gas that spirals in from far away to the inner edge has released an energy equal to

$$ 1 - \sqrt{8/9} = 5{,}7\% $$

of its rest mass. Hydrogen fusion in the Sun’s core releases only 0.7%. That 8-fold efficiency is why black holes that are “feeding” on gas can outshine entire galaxies.

+++ Going deeper: finding 3 rs and $\sqrt{8/9}$
Circular orbits sit at a peak or at the bottom of a well of $V(r)$. Using $G = c = 1$, set $\dd V/\dd r = 0$:

$$ \frac{M}{r^2} - \frac{L^2}{r^3} + \frac{3ML^2}{r^4} = 0 $$

$$ \Rightarrow\; Mr^2 - L^2r + 3ML^2 = 0 $$

$$ r = \frac{L^2}{2M}\Big(1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 12M^2/L^2}\Big) $$

The plus sign is the bottom (stable), the minus sign the peak (unstable). For example, with $L = 2{,}13\,r_sc$ the bottom is at 7.18 rs and the peak at 1.90 rs. When $L^2 = 12M^2$ the two roots merge at $r = L^2/2M = 6M = 3\,r_s$. Any smaller and there is no root at all: no more circular orbits.

The energy there is $E^2 = (1 - r_s/r)(1 + L^2/r^2) = \frac23\cdot\frac43 = \frac89$. At rest very far away, $E = 1$. The part lost is $1 - \sqrt{8/9} = 0{,}057$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.ten: Falling in: a world line that never turns back
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
This time the object is released from 12 rs with too little angular momentum. On the graph the yellow line lies **above the peak** of the blue curve: there is no wall to stop it. The object loops almost once around and then crosses the horizon.

Look at the world line. The nearer it gets to the horizon tube, the steeper the spring becomes and the more closely it hugs the tube. According to the distant clock, the object **never** reaches the horizon; the light it sends to our eyes arrives slower and slower, redder and redder, fainter and fainter.

But the object’s own clock (in the data box) runs on for only a finite time more. By that clock, the object crosses the horizon and notices nothing special there. The two statements do not contradict each other: the coordinate $t$ of the distant clock cannot be used right at the horizon. Lesson 16 switches to different coordinates to draw the whole world line passing through.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the velocity arrow to launch the object yourself: aim it outward but slowly, and it still turns back and falls in; aim it sideways and fast enough, and it loops around and escapes.
> [[See the world line|ktg]] [[See it on Flamm’s paraboloid|mat]]

> [Tóm lại]
> | Kind of orbit | On the effective-potential graph |
> |---|---|
> | Slowly turning ellipse | the energy line cuts the well at two points |
> | Stable circle | the energy line touches the bottom of the well |
> | Zoom-whirl, then fly out | the energy line is just below the peak |
> | Falling in | the energy line is above the peak |
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.thuThach.de: Launch the object **outward**, away from the black hole (arrow tilted outward, outward component at least 5% of c), and still have it turn back and fall through the horizon.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.thuThach.goiY: Flying outward without enough energy (E less than 1), the object must turn back. If the sideways component is also small, the angular momentum is small, the energy line lies above the peak of the potential and nothing stops the fall. Try 10% of c outward and 8% of c sideways.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.ten: The Schwarzschild metric in the orbital plane
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: $r_s = 2GM/c^2$; $t$ is the time of a clock very far away.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: They exist because the metric does not change with time or with rotation about the center.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: The last term is Einstein’s addition; it keeps the ellipse from closing.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.5.y: Efficiency of energy release in a gas disk: $1-\sqrt{8/9} = 5{,}7\%$.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: According to general relativity, why does a planet’s ellipse not close?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.1: Because the Sun also moves around the center of the Milky Way
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.2: Because the term $-GML^2/(c^2r^3)$ makes the in-and-out period longer than one revolution
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.3: Because the other planets tug on it
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.4: Because light from the planet takes time to reach Earth
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: In Newton’s theory, going in and out and going once around take exactly the same time, so the ellipse closes. Einstein’s term slows the in-and-out oscillation slightly, so the object goes more than once around before it returns to the closest point. The other planets **also** make Mercury’s perihelion turn, but Newton could already calculate that part; the 43″ is what is left over.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: A planet has the same eccentricity as Mercury but a semi-major axis 4 times larger. What is its general-relativistic precession **per century**?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: Per orbit, the turning angle is proportional to $1/a$: 4 times smaller. But the period is proportional to $a^{3/2}$ (Kepler’s third law): 8 times longer, so a century holds 8 times fewer orbits. Together: $4 \times 8 = 32$ times smaller. People often forget the number of orbits per century.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: The orbit in the model has specific energy $E = 0{,}973$. What does this number tell you?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.1: The object moves at 97.3% of the speed of light
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.2: The object is bound to the black hole and cannot get very far away
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.3: The object is about to fall into the black hole
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.4: The object’s clock runs at 97.3% of the rate of a distant clock
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: $E$ is measured in units of the rest energy $mc^2$. Reaching very far away (and stopping there) requires $E \ge 1$. $E \lt 1$ means the orbit is bound. $E$ is neither a speed nor a clock rate: the rate of the object’s clock changes continuously along the orbit.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: Why does a gas disk around a non-rotating black hole have an inner edge at about 3 rs?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: Because the temperature there is so high that all the gas evaporates
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: Because there are no stable circular orbits inside 3 rs: the gas spirals straight in
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.3: Because 3 rs is the event horizon
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.4: Because light cannot escape from below 3 rs
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: The horizon is at 1 rs and the photon sphere at 1.5 rs; light can still escape from 3 rs. The inner edge comes from orbital mechanics: below 3 rs the well and the peak of the effective potential have merged, so every circular orbit is unstable.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: An object falls into a black hole. Which statement is correct?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.1: By the object’s own clock, it takes forever to reach the horizon
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: By the distant clock, the object crosses the horizon after a finite time
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.3: By the object’s own clock, it crosses the horizon after a finite time; a distant observer sees it slow down forever
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.4: The object is stopped at the horizon by an enormous force
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: The object’s proper time to reach the horizon is finite. The time $t$ of the distant clock grows without limit, because the coordinate $t$ breaks down exactly at the horizon. There is no wall at the horizon; for a large black hole the object crosses it without feeling anything special.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: Explain in your own words: “Mercury moves straight, but we see it go around.”
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: Mercury is in free fall, so its world line is a geodesic: the “straightest” path through the curved spacetime around the Sun, in the sense that it makes proper time longest. That path is a spring stretched along the time axis, almost straight at true scale. What we call the orbit is only its shadow in three-dimensional space: a nearly closed ellipse. Because spacetime is curved exactly as the Schwarzschild metric says, that shadow slowly turns by 43″ per century.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapter 9: orbits in the Schwarzschild geometry, the effective potential, the innermost stable circular orbit; chapter 10: the perihelion precession of Mercury.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: E. F. Taylor, J. A. Wheeler and E. Bertschinger, *Exploring Black Holes* (2nd edition): energy, angular momentum and orbits around black holes, written for beginners.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: B. Schutz, *A First Course in General Relativity* (2nd edition, 2009): the section on orbits of massive particles in the Schwarzschild geometry.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: GRAVITY Collaboration 2020, A&A 636, L5: measurement of the precession of the star S2 around Sagittarius A*.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: The function $V(r)$ that combines the attraction with the “centrifugal” part due to rotation, so that radial motion looks like a marble rolling on a slope. Einstein adds the term $-GML^2/(c^2r^3)$.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: An object’s energy divided by $mc^2$; it stays fixed along a geodesic because the metric does not change with time. Below 1: the object is bound.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: An object’s angular momentum divided by its mass, $L = r^2\,\dd\varphi/\dd\tau$; it stays fixed because the metric does not change under rotation about the center.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: An orbit whose energy is just below the peak of the effective potential: the object whirls several times close to the black hole before zooming back out. Newton’s theory has no such orbit.
